utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I should say, for the benefit of the transcript, that this evidence is being heard by videolink. Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Sir, could you please begin by telling us your name and your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: My name is Sefik Beslic. I was born on the 29th of January 1951 in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Doctor, my name is John Docherty. I am one of the prosecuting attorneys on this case. I don't believe we have met before, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: No, we have not. That is right, we have never met.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have no transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: There will be a few seconds delay, Doctor, while we deal with a technical problem at our end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We must have a transcript, is that correct, Mr. Docherty?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I believe so, Your Honour, otherwise, there will be no record. That is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I understand the technical problem has been resolved, and it should be just stated that we have been delayed because of this technical problem. Yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Good morning again, Witness. I apologise for that. There is a lot of technology here. It usually works faultlessly, but every once in a while there is a glitch. You had stated your state your name and date of birth for the record. Could you continue, please, by telling us what it is that you do for a living.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: I am head of the department of oncological surgery in Sarajevo. During the war, I was -- during the war, or rather, for 12 years, I was the top surgeon at abdominal surgery, and now I'm in the department of oncology surgery; the surgery of tumours, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Doctor, in what year did you graduate from medical school or obtain your medical degree?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: I completed my studies in 1976.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And could you tell the Court, please, briefly, the training that you under went and experience you had in order to become head of abdominal surgery, which is the position you have testified you held during war?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: Before the war, let me tell you exactly. From 1980, I was at the department of surgery, so practically for 12 years I had been a surgeon. During my work at the surgery department, I went for advanced training, specialist training. I went to England four times. I was in Manchester in 1985/1986. I spent two months there then; then in 1988, I was there, I think, for two and a half months. I can't remember now. Then in 1989, I spent a month there; and in 1990/1991, I spent five months and I returned from Manchester to Sarajevo in 1991. Doing my work the way I did, I also developed in terms of my career.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Doctor, when you say that you are head of abdominal surgery, could you tell us in which hospital in Sarajevo you were head of abdominal surgery?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: This is the Clinical Centre in Sarajevo where I have been working for day one. That is where I had my first job. So for the first two years, I worked in intensive care, that was in 1978 and 1979. From 1980, I worked at abdominal surgery all the way up to 1994 -- no, sorry, 2004, when I transferred to oncology surgery. All three years I worked as an abdominal surgery, and now I work as an oncology surgeon. But for the most part, I do abdominal surgery, again, in that field, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And, Doctor, I'm going to turn to a specific operation that you performed on 18th of November of 1994. To begin with, did you give a statement to an investigator and a prosecuting attorney from this Tribunal on January the 30th of 2007?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't remember the exact date but yes, I did give a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And over the last few days, have you had an opportunity to read the summary of that statement in a language which you understand?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: When you did that review, did you find the summary to be an accurate reflection of what you had said on 30th of January this year?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: Yes. All of that is correct, but I did notice one mistake, which I didn't even see at that time, because I didn't have an opportunity of seeing the document then. My statement was the way I gave it. However, I had a look at the papers from the operation that was carried out at the time, and I looked at the history recorded by the doctor and a small mistake was made then. For me it's a small mistake, but probably --.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Well, for the sake of thoroughness, could you tell what that small mistake is, please.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: Well, after 13 years or 12 and a half years after that operation that I carried out myself, I could not recall the case. But when they gave me the operational findings that I had written down myself and the medical history that was written down by my young colleague, I saw that he replaced some pages. There are scars on the abdomen of the lady, the patient involved. The projectile entered the right side and got out on the left side, exited through the left side. This is information that is clear to all who have ever had anything to do with war surgery, so if the patient was operated on the right side, or rather, the bullet entered the right side and exited on the left side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And, Doctor, with that --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, could the witness in Sarajevo be shown and on e-court here be displayed the first page of 65 ter number 03058, which is the statement in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Just one question, I'm trying not to flood the Chambers with documents that are already in our file. The documents -- 65 ter documents 3077, 3078 are included in a document which has already been admitted in is D19. So I'm talking about the pages of these documents, and they're on the Defence list. And the Defence is going to use these documents with this witness, and it's on column 1D on the Defence list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: That is not the document that I have called for at this time. I have called fort statement, and I think Ms. Isailovic is referring to some pages from the medical documentation, which I will get to in a few minutes after we've got the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Well, that clarifies it. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So I had asked for 65 ter number 03058, if the witness in Sarajevo could be shown the hard copy and if we could see the first e-court page displayed here in The Hague, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Dr. Beslic, do you have the first page -- do you have your statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: I have the statement. These are my details, my particulars. Now I have it, yes. Could I just read it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Certainly. Take a moment and read it.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: And I fully agree with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender this statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P521, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Dr. Beslic, just a few clarifying questions and then we will be finished. According to the records that you were shown, you operated on Dzenana Sokolovic on 18th of November of 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Approximately how many times in your career, Doctor, have you operated on people who are suffering from gunshot wounds?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number; however, perhaps it was the largest one of all who worked in the hospital where I worked. I cannot give you the exact number, but it's a very big number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And based upon your experience --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The Interpreter could not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue with what you were saying before you stopped.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to say that out of this large number of patients that we had, at that time we just really wanted to help as much as possible. I really did not think about the number of patients at all because practically I lived at the hospital all the time, and I worked every day. I operated on people every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. What I wanted to ask next was whether based upon your training, upon your experience with gunshot victims, and upon your review of the medical documentation, you could tell us which side of Dzenana Sokolovic was the entrance wound on?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: On the right side, because it was smaller. And on the left side was the exit wound where the wound is larger, which shows that the projectile went from right to left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And in addition to your training, your experience, and a review of the file, did you also have occasion to physically examine Dzenana Sokolovic at the request of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: The same day when I talked to them, they brought her in the evening and I examined her.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And was there anything about that examination that contradicted your view that the bullet entered her on the right side?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: Nothing. My conclusion is the same as the one given in the statement of mine; that is to say, during this examination, I established and confirmed the findings included in my operation findings at the time; that is to say, that the bullet entered on the right side and exited on the left side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When was that examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Doctor, you said that they -- they brought her on the same day. Are you referring, then, sir, to the day on which you gave your statement?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I gave my statement -- or rather, the first time they came to see me, we agreed on 12.00, midday, because I had to finish my operations programme. They came to see me around 12.00 and I said, "For me to be in a position to give you accurate data, I would have to see the patient because I do not recall the case." Then they agreed to bring the patient in that evening at 6.00, so then I came there at 6.00 on the same day. I examined the lady, the patient involved, and confirmed the original findings I made.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And just to clear up any ambiguity, Doctor, this all occurred, the giving of statement and the examination of the patient all occurred on the same day?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, I understand that from reviewing the medical file, and there are some pages referred to in your statement by the index numbers that we use here at the Tribunal, that you looked at two pages concerning this case that I particularly want to focus attention on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And if the - excuse me one moment, Your Honour - witness could please be shown ERN pages 0028-4033 and 0028-4034. Your Honour, those are in our exhibit spreadsheet as 65 ter 1484A. The B/C/S versions of that 65 ter number are very difficult to read, and the ERNs that I have just read out are identical to what we have in B/C/S, except that they are much better copies. So yesterday evening we made arrangements to have those shown to the witness. The English versions in the binder with which you have been provided are fine, as far as legibility goes. I don't see Dr. Beslic on the screen. May I inquire if he has the medical documents in front of him. There he is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Doctor, did you review -- is that part of the medical --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: We don't have them on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can they be put on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: The page I am looking for, Your Honour, is -- it's in 65 ter 1484A, and it is the third e-court page in the English. I believe, Your Honour, that these are the pages that Ms. Isailovic made reference to earlier. The page on the screen -- I'm sorry. I might be getting the e-court pages mixed up, but we're looking for ERN RR 251210. I'm sorry to do this, but could we go back one page before this in sequence, 1209. Is there an English translation of that, an ET? Thank you. I apologise for that, Your Honour. I was working with these documents up until a few minutes before coming to court and I'm afraid it shows.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Doctor, in the papers that you have just had the opportunity to review, is there a notation there from a colleague of yours in the emergency department or casualty ward?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: Where it gives the operation finding, there is a history, a medical history and an anamnesis, and I see that it is written by hand. This is usually noted down when the patient is allowed to go home.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Do you also see a little below the anamnesis, the Latin "status praesens," and below that the notation concerning the entrance and exit wounds of this gunshot injury?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: The only place I see the entry and exit wound mentioned is in the part of the text coming under the heading of "Case History," the status praesens, in the part where the abdomen is described, it says that the wound is part of the paramedial left which is smaller than the paramedial right wound. That is what it says, but this is an error. This is an error. So the sides have been switched because you can see on the patient that it's the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Two questions about this entry in status praesens, Doctor. First of all, are these your notes or the notes of a colleague.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: This was noted down by my colleague, Dr. Sabanovic. I can see his name there. He is a young doctor who started working in the hospital a year before this happened. It was they who wrote down the case history information for every patient --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: -- because we didn't have time to do that, as we were always in the operating room. And these young doctors would write down the information and come and assist us during the operation. This was a young colleague. I didn't even know him at the time. They were novices in our ward. The colleague who wrote this down is still working. He specialised in abdominal surgery later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And, Dr. Beslic, you may have already answered this, but my second question concerning this note is based on your experience working in the clinical centre during the war, do you have an opinion as to how it is that you your colleague, Dr. Sabanovic, could have got the left and the right reversed, as it is your opinion happened in this case?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: There's a very simple answer to that question. We had large numbers of patients with wounds, and it was mostly the young doctors who noted down the information. They might look at two or three patients at a time, write down information, and then going and make these notes, and then he might have switched the sides. Since to us at that time, it didn't matter whether it was the right or the left side. We just wanted to help the patients, because very often people would die before they reached the operating theatre, and sometimes this information would have to be written down even after the operation. It was not the case here because this woman was not that badly wounded, so he might have been taking down notes for several case histories at a tile. I'm not sure, but at that time it didn't seem important us whether it was the left or right side because I would have to look at the patient before the operation anyway, and I didn't read the notes then because they meant nothing to me at the time. I didn't need them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Beslic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I have no further questions on direct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I wanted to ask the doctor a question about the last point that he raised. Doctor, you said that the doctor who wrote these notes was young, he had been only working in the hospital for one year. And I wondered whether there was any procedure --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- any procedure by which what he wrote would have been reviewed whether by you or by anybody else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no such procedure. In the circumstances we were working in, in wartime, believe me, it was the last thing on our minds, because we would look at the patients, and those young doctors would do the formal administrative tasks and deal with the documents. It was only the finding of the operation that was important. In these documents, there were always possibilities of making mistakes, but the documentation of the operation was always correct. And it could always be checked on the patient, and thank God this patient has survived so she can be examined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Thank you, Doctor. Judge Mindua has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness, with this mistake, we're really at the very heart of the incident. Your explanation is that your young colleague just made a mistake between pages, but I don't really understand this idea of pages. Because here we have two lines saying the entry point, 0.5 centimetre wide, is to the left and the exit point wound, three times two centimetres, to the paramedian right and bleeding. And you gave us a very simple rule. You said that the entry wound is small and the exit wound is bigger. So could you please tell us and explain what your young colleague actually did not understand. He didn't know that the entry point was small and the exit wound was big? Is that what he mistook or this problem of pages. I can't match the pages with the problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one small thing I would like so add. I'm listening to the two versions, and the French interpreter said "pages" because he did not get the end of the sentence, but it was "sides" and not "pages." But can you listen to the explanation from the doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In B/C/S, the word for page and the word for side is the same, and interpreters might have misunderstood the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, you should answer the question now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's like this: The central line that we use to orient ourselves, it wasn't referring to pages but to the right and left side of the central line, and then there is a cut that I made. There were injuries on both the left and the right side of that central line. The entry wound, unfortunately, there's an error here, because here it says that the wound on the right side was larger that the one on the left. But when you look at the patient, you can see that the entry wound is on the right side and that it's smaller. It's about the size noted here, and the exit wound which is on the left side, which is larger, can be seen quite easily on the patient. So that the patient is what we should lock at. Anyone can make a mistake, but you cannot make a mistake when you look at the patient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. I'm Branislava Isailovic, member of the Paris bar, and I am defending the accused in these proceedings, General Dragomir Milosevic. I'm going to ask you a few questions regarding your statement and the medical reports that you have just commented. So, first, I will use document D19, which is a document that has already been admitted, and page 10 of this document; ERN RR 251208 for the B/C/S version, and 00284032 for the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, my first question is as follows: It seems that this page and the following page of the document, RR 251209, are part of a single document, and this is not obvious in the bundle that we were given. Can you confirm that these are two pages of the same document?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: I don't know which document. This one?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe I could --

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: The finding I'm looking at is the letter of discharge and I fully agree with it, and it's the original one.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: To make sure that we don't mistake anything, I am asking you to look at document RR 251208 and to confirm that on the right angle, it says "historija bolesti"?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: I don't know which document you are referring to. Oh, yes. I have this document before me, but that is not the number it has on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that the document you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have D19. This is the document I am using. But the numbers have just been given, I don't know anything about them, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There seems to be some confusion. I understand that the counsel wants the witness to confirm that two pages belong to the same document. Is that it? Yes, tell us what --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tell us first what are the two pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the first one is on the right side off the screen, RR 251208, that is the ERN number. And the second page is the e-court number 11 of document D19, RR 251209. The two pages we have on the screen now. The first is on the right-hand side and the second page is on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, maybe you can clarify the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I think so, Your Honour. This relates to the legibility issue that I was talking about at the beginning of my direct examination where the B/C/S pages of some of these documents are very hard to read, and I can go through and give the old ERN and what the one is that the witness now has, if that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, if you can resolve it, you will have a prize.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay. RR 251205 and 1206 were perfectly legible and were left alone. RR 251207 was replaced with 00284031; RR 251208 was replaced with 00284032; RR 251209 was replaced with 00284033; and, finally, RR 251210 was replaced with 00284034.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that helpful to the officer in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I'm concerned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me hear the officer in Sarajevo. Are you understanding it better now?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And are we now able to have presented to the witness the two pages that counsel has referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are these the two pages?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, the witness has the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness has the document, and the question was whether the witness can confirm that those two pages are two pages of the same document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. Yes, these are two pages of the same document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, could you also confirm that this document called historija bolesti, written on November 25th, 1994, so it was written when the patient actually left the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: That's correct. This is a document which is written when the patient is discharged from hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Please, could you give us some explanation about the documents used to actually draft this historija bolesti?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I didn't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: This document, historija bolesti, is written when the patient leaves the hospital. Normally that is the case for all patients?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: Yes, one page. It's just a front page. The historija bolesti is taken down when the patient is admitted. That is the part where it says "anamnesis." That is a document that is written when the patient is admitted to hospital. However, the front page is written when the patient is released from hospital or discharged.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But are these two pages part of a bundle of documents?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: That is just one piece of paper. It's separated here, but it's actually one sheet of paper which consists of two pages, two sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Just to make things accurate, it's on both pages of a document. Is it one single page written on one side and the other side?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: Correct, correct. No, they are two pages. It's folded. A paper is folded. The front page is where it says "historija bolesti," and then when you open it on the inside or it can be on the outside, whatever side they use, but it's two pages in one piece. It's one sheet of paper folded over and consisting of two pages. The front page where it says "historija bolesti" and the second page where it says "anamnesis."

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So could we say that it is like a file that is used to slip other documents into this file?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: Correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now I have a -- now that we have cleared that, I have another question. You said that one page is written when the patient is admitted into the hospital and the other one when the patient leaves the hospital. Could you please tell us who writes the first page of the document, the one that starts with "anamnesis"?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: Most often, but not as a rule, however, most often, it is written by the people who sign it. It's the younger doctors, the junior doctors, and the name of the doctor who filled in that page is noted here. In this case, it's Dr. Sabanovic. It says that at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: We can't see anything. Witness, have you been able to see the original of this document?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: I have this document before me, and you can see that Dr. Sabanovic's name is noted down here, on the right-hand side at the bottom. This is the page?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So, Dr. Sabanovic at the time the patient is admitted into hospital, this is Mrs. Sokolovic in this case, the entire page is then written down, the page which contains the heading "anamnesis" and "status present." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: These are the details of that patient, although her name is not written down here because this consists of two pages. And the name of the patient, Dzenana Sokolovic is on the front page with all her details taken down by the people in our administration. So the upper part of the front page contains her name, her place of birth, her profession, her address, and so on. And that is noted down by a member of the administrative staff. The anamnesis was written down by Dr. Sabanovic and the last bit on the front page where it says "epikriza," that's written by another doctor. In this case, it is Dr. Secic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, at the time Dr. Sabanovic was writing the second page, did he see the patient?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: He should have seen her. I'm sure he saw her because the anamnesis has to be written down by someone who has seen the patient.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So the sentence which starts with "[B/C/S spoken]" [No interpretation] Witness, Dr. Sabanovic examined the patient and was able to therefore write these things down in the document. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to note for the record that when counsel spoke a paragraph or two of B/C/S a moment ago there was no translation of it. I don't know if it -- if it's important to Ms. Isailovic, I think she was just using that to direct the witness to a particular point on the page, but there was no translation. And if that is important to her cross-examination, that may need to be rectified, the substance of it, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Isailovic, if you wish to repeat the question, do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know why this has happened, why we have no translation. Is it -- does it depend on which channel one is on? If I repeat the question in the same way, will it be recorded on the transcript or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It will be recorded. Just repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So my question runs as follows: Can you turn to the turn to the second page the sentence that reads: "To the left paramedially, there is visible an entry wound, size 0.5 centimetres, which is bleeding; and paramedially to the right, there is visible an exit wound, 3 by 2 centimetres in size, which is bleeding." Mr. Sabanovic wrote this down after having examined the patient. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested to know how you made up your mind about the mistake that was made by Dr. Sabanovic. Could you explain this to us a little bit, please?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: It's very simply. Everything can be seen on the patient, so the findings are the other way around when you see the patient herself. Evidently he made a mistake. Such mistakes occur even today in peacetime, not in a state of war when you have five, seven, ten people who come in at the same time, wounded. This part didn't really mean anything to me. I hadn't even checked it. And if you had not brought it up, I never would have realised it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Doctor, there is at least one part of Dr. Sabanovic's statement which is consistent, it seems to me, with your evidence today, and it is that the size of the entry wound is smaller than the size of the exit wound.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So the only thing that is wrong is the side, whether it is the right or left.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. However, all of this can be seen on the patient herself. You can see it very nicely on the patient. On the right side, a smaller entry wound; and on the left side, a larger exit wound. And that is the most reliable information.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, when you can see that you see that the best possible way on the patient herself, can you explain this to us what can you see on the patient?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: On the patient herself, you can see the scars; on the right side the smaller one from the entry wound, and on the left side, the larger one from the exit wounds. So it is reverse in relation to what was written on the document at the time, which means that my colleague confused the sides at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, as you are a doctor with a wealth experience and some remarkable training, you obviously know about deformed scars, malformations that can occur where the scar is after 12 years?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: Theoretically, there can be changes. It cannot be decreased; perhaps it can be increased. And the woman would have had another operation in order for that to happen, because the scars on the patient correspond to what it was that had actually occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And how do you know that there had been no intervention on the patient?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: That I don't know. That is true. That I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, to reverse something which has been written down by one of your colleagues, you are doing this on the basis of something which you are unsure about, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: I'm basing this on the findings that I reached on the basis of examining the patient.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But you know that your colleague wrote something down, and the colleague also based his findings after having seen the patient.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: That's correct. That is correct. That is what he wrote, but there was this possibility for him to have made a mistake. I'm saying that on the basis of experience, because throughout the world there is this possibility of making a mistake of that kind, even in peacetime. And in America, for instance, they think that surgeons can make mistakes that exceed those that are made by others. So in a state of war, you can see where the shooting took place, and can you see where this was being recorded, perhaps in the dark. So a mistake was possible. Of course, I cannot swear there was no plastic surgery after wards, as you said. But this is a small scar which is typical for an entry wound that is not clean. It's a wound from a bullet or something, or it can be shrapnel, too. But in this case, it is most probably a bullet wound because shrapnel gives a different picture. However, if you look at the scar itself, it's jagged, so that means that it was not operated on later. However, I cannot swear on the operative finding and also what I see on the document, but then the young doctor confused the sides on his document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it fair to say, Witness, that it's now for the first time, and when you answer my question, that it's the first time that you actually raise this question and think about it that maybe an intervention was performed on the scars?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: I had no dilemma with the scars because that was typical for the scars that I saw after injuries, after woundings sustained by a bullet. These wounds are not processed in that way because they are dirty, so they are jagged. They are very irregular. For a plastic surgeon to have dealt with this, that really does not fit into what I see today by way of my own findings.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But you said, if I understood you correctly, "I cannot swear that this is the case." Didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot swear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry. Counsel is on his feet. Let me hear what he has to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I object to this question being put. The witness has been asked question and answered the question just put to him, I think, about four times now, and this really has become arguing with the witness, rather than examining the witness. And I object to counsel continuing to ask "isn't it possible that."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no. What she is doing I think is quite proper. She is reminding him that earlier, and I do recollect myself, that he said that he cannot swear that in the event that there had been a surgical intervention in the last 12 years, that there might not have been some change in the scar, and she is reminding of that testimony. I think she is entitled to do that. Yes, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Docherty interrupted the witness while he was answering, perhaps the witness could finish his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said the scar was typical for a bullet injury; so, a wound that was not sewn up because it was dirty. That is why it is so irregular. Practically this scar could be removed so that it is not even there any longer. However, I don't think that a single plastic surgeon anywhere in the world would be able to conduct surgery to make it look the way it looks now, in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, a while ago you said that these documents, as a rule, were drafted by junior colleagues that had little experience, and that the latter could make mistakes when they drafted these medical documents in your clinic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: According to you, as at the time you were the head of this clinic, can you tell us whether one can rely on these documents that were drafted by your junior colleagues in your clinic, if they did not know the difference between one side and another of the human body or other matters perhaps also?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, I believe that we have heard enough evidence now to determine the reliability of the kind of information that the junior colleague would have given. I don't think it is for the witness to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You examined Mrs. Sokolovic again. Were you the only person who dealt with this examination or not?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall who else was there, but the findings were important to me, in n terms of the surgical findings. And what really mattered to me was that the woman survives, and whether it was the left or the right was irrelevant at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, but I was actually thinking about something else. An examination which was performed on the 30th of January in Sarajevo of that same year, were you the sole physician conducting the examination?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: I was the only physician, because I could not call in the people who were with me. I could only have medical staff present there. I was there and there nurse was there. I couldn't really invite anyone else in, as the woman had to undress and I had to examine her.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, you didn't take any pictures of her scars, did you?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't take any pictures because I don't take pictures of other patients either. And, first of all, the patient would have had to allow me to do so, and it never crossed my mind at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is this: This woman's scars, could you tell us a little bit where these scars are located, those scars that you were able to examine on the 30th of January?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: The scars on the spot that is described in the findings that I have, on the left and the right paramedially; that is to say, to the left and the right of the operation cut that was made in the middle of the abdomen.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And, Witness, if you draw a straight line between these two points, and if we imagine that this person, Mrs. Sokolovic, is standing, now the line that we have drawn between the exit wound and entry wound, what kind of angle is there between that line and the ground?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let me hear. Witness, please, refrain from answering, because counsel is on his feet. Ms. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe where we are going with this is an effort to draw from the evidence more than it will bear. As you will recall, Mr. Van den Weijden was here last Friday and was asked a number of questions about having to know the attitude of the body at that time that a bullet hit it, and I believe therefore that this is going beyond the -- the immediate question does not go off course beyond the doctor's competence, but my concern is with the questions that I think are inevitably going follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is it that you are seeking to establish, Ms. Isailovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the same as the Prosecutor. So as we have this witness via videolink, and this man is a doctor and has seen the scars because none of have seen the scars. Therefore, I would like him to tell us because we don't have any photographs, and we have to rely on the document. We have a document but it is questionable. So in the event that Dr. Beslic's testimony is reliable, why can't we have his testimony as an eye-witness, because he was a person who saw the patient on the 30th of January after the physician who examined her in 1994, Mr. Sabanovic, but we realised that Dr. Sabanovic has made a mistake. So if he has seen the scars, that's what -- that's precisely what I'm interested in and where are the scars located. Are they at the level of the stomach? Where are they, and what has he seen on the patient?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber will allow the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, would you like me it repeat the question? Have you understood my question?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: I understood the question full well; however, this information about the angle. First of all, I don't even know what patient was in when she was wounded so it is very hard to say that. However, it is obvious, it is quite clear, to the left and to the right of the surgical cut, the exit and the entry wound. I cannot tell you about centimetres during the surgery or now, but, say, it's about ten centimetres from the middle line to the left, right. What the position was, under what angle it was, let mathematicians calculate that. I really don't know that. They are parallel practically. Perhaps a centimetre up or done. I don't know. That detail I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. You were interrupted by the Prosecutor's question, and I shall therefore repeat my question. You said you don't know and I don't either and the Trial Chamber doesn't know either, so we have to establish the truth here. You are the only person who has actually seen the scars of Mrs. Sokolovic on the 30th of January. What I'm interested in is to know whether Mrs. Sokolovic was standing up, and from the ground upwards where were her scars located? I'm not interested in the angle. I'm not interested in anything of that kind.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: In order to answer that question, I would have to know how tall the woman is. I haven't got her dimensions. I really don't know how tall the women is, and I don't know what distances are involved. I really cannot give you that answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm -- it's extremely important me. I'm sorry. I shall ask the question again in B/C/S, because I think that -- and then I shall check the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, what I do not understand in your question is exactly what you are looking for. Is it the question of whether the line between the entry wound and the exit wound is horizontal, or is it the number of centimetres from the ground up until that line? What is it that you are really looking for? And, regardless of which of the two questions you're putting really, what is the importance that? That I do not understand. Can you explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honours, I didn't have time to check the translation, but it's precisely the height. No matter how high, but the height and where the scars. You said parallel scars. Perhaps one could say it that way. That's how I was started off. I was quite ambitious. So if you draw a line between the two exit and entry wounds, you have a straight line, and is this straight line parallel to the ground? That was my first question. Is it parallel to the ground or not when the patient is standing up? And, now, this is why my question is important, it is most important afterwards with the rest of the evidence we have had in support of this incident. We have had a lot of evidence that has been compared, and we can draw the conclusion and see which -- where the shot was fired from, and the potential location of a shooter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Isailovic, the original question which you asked was not very clear. Now the question is clearer. But notwithstanding that, I believe that the witness has answered the question by saying that perhaps there was a differential of one or two centimetres, and that the line between entry and exit wound was more or less horizontal.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for what you have said. This is what I understood, but I'm not sure it was clear to everyone, because I didn't check it out. This is why I wanted to put the question in B/C/S again, but if that is what has been understood in English that's fine by me. That is in fact the answer I wish to hear. Now I would like to see the rest of the document that we were looking at and that is -- I shall use the pages I have, and that is documents D12, RR 251210.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Surgery, operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you have this page in front of you? Can you see it? And do we have it on our screens? This page is not included in the set of documents or in the document we've just talked about. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And as I can see here on the photocopy, this is an excerpt, I believe, from a log-book or something. Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, possibly. Possibly, yes. It's clear. It can be seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us where this comes from, what kind of register or book or log-book?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: I don't know. You're referring to the perforations here. I really don't know. Perhaps that was something that was subsequently inserted. I don't remember papers being filed this way. I told you that these two pages, the surgery itself and the history -- the medical history, they were usually on a single sheet that was folded. Perhaps these were photocopies. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: According to what you know, this "operativni zahvat," this sheet of paper, generally speaking, where is it filed in a patient's medical file?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: What do you mean where it was? While the patient was still in our hospital, we still had the document. After that, the document is sent to archives; then I really don't know what happens after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, we are at the time for the break. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, you should be bringing the cross-examination to a close now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will do that, and I will bring it to a close quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, we looked at the document, "operativni zahvat." Do you have it close by?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us when this document is written during the procedure?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: It's written immediately after the surgery.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: What you have just said, does this relate to the totality of the document or only to the part that is typewritten with a typewriter?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: Only the part that is typed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And the rest of the observations that are written on the document, could you tell us exactly who writes these handwritten marks?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: Usually junior doctors. It might all have been written down by Dr. Sabanovic, because letters of discharge are usually written by junior doctors. Both admission and discharge are usually written by junior doctors.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, you're saying that these documents, "operativni zahvat," those are documents that are written by the young doctors, the juniors?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: Operativni zahvat is, as a rule, written by the doctor who did the surgery. The other handwritten notes are made while the patient is lying in hospital and just before the patient is discharged, and you can see the dates of these notes, the 21st, the 15th, or whatever. That is before the patient went home. It says that stitches were removed, so that is just before we went home; and in every hospital, it is junior doctors who make these notes. It's not just in Sarajevo in wartime. It's like that everywhere. It was like that in England as well. Wherever I worked abroad, the procedure was similar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So this typewritten part, did you originally draft the typewritten part?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: Most probably, yes. Most probably, it was either I or I may have dictated to a colleague. Those are the two possibilities. I can't recall precisely. Either did I it myself or I dictated and he typed it out.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: The B/C/S version is not very legible, but I'm -- I believe that you have the original under -- at hand, and I also have a copy that is not very legible. Could you please write -- could you please read what is written under "op nalaz"?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: By --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness be asked to read slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, just a minute. You have to read more slowly for the benefit of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, all right. "Bimedial laparotomy," which means by a medial cut, a cut down the middle, "there was opened the stomach layer by layer, and there was found only on the liver, on the fourth segment, a contusion from a blast. While, on the other organs, no pathological changes were found. The abdomen was then" -- I assume it says here "closed," but there are some letters missing, "and the wound was dressed and then drainage applied." There are a few grammatical mistakes here. The way "drainage" is spelled, for example.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can I conclude from this that the scar on the patient's body are not only the entry and exit wounds, but there is also the scar of where you actually opened the abdomen between these two points?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: The abdomen was not opened between the two points, the entry and exit wound. It was opened down the middle and the wounds were on either side of the cut. So length-wise from the middle of the rib arch downwards was the surgical cut; whereas, the round wounds were at either side, to the right and to the left of the cut.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement that was shown to you by the Prosecutor and just has been admitted, in paragraph 3 --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please have the statement shown to the witness. This is 65 ter document 3058, which has been given the number P524 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 521.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: On page 2, please, on paragraph 3, at the end of the paragraph, you are talking about this contusion, this contusion of the liver that you have just mentioned while you were reading.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: This is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I believe that in your statement you are believing that the contusion is the consequence of an effect, and a consequence of the bullet that came into the abdomen of Mrs. Sokolovic and actually went through her whole -- through her entire stomach?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So I would like you to answer by yes or no to my question: This bullet that is going through the body, isn't that that actually has the contusion as a consequence?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So could you please explain the relationship between the entry point -- if the entry point is close to the exit point, could you tell us exactly how you determine the entry point using the passage of the bullet. Can you explain the logic that you actually determine where the entry wound was, in relation to the contusion?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: It's very simple, especially for someone who knows what this looks like. It passed from the -- it passed down the lower side of the liver. I didn't say the entry and exit wounds were close by, because one was on one side and the other was on the other side. So the bullet passed right next to the liver and caused a blastoma, most probably a hematoma on that side, and then exited on the other side. It is quite simple when you see it, especially if you know what all this looks like. When one sees the patient, everything is clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You explained this very well, and everything is very clear. But my question is the following: Whichever entry or exit wound, I think it's the passage of the bullet next to the liver that actually leads to the contusion. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK BESLIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I have no re-examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Dr. Beslic, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for giving it and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next witness is also by video-conference link.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And that will be handled by my colleague, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we're waiting for the next witness, I should mention that we had hoped to have three witnesses today, just as we had hoped to have another witness yesterday. Without going into detail, we are continuing to have serious problems, let us say, procuring the attendance of this witness, and so the witness about to appear will, I'm sorry to say, be the last one for today. However, we continue to take the view that there will be no difficulty in concluding all of the videolink witnesses on schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thursday is our last day here. Friday being Good Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes. And I had that in mind when I gave that statement, Your Honour. If we were able to procure this witness, we will shoehorn that person in somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you may begin, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can I first ask you whether you can hear me in a language that you understand and that you can see me as well on the screen.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And can I ask to you please state your full name, your place, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Andja Gotovac; 23rd of March, 1930; born in Travnik --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: -- in Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I just want to tell that you my name is Manoj Sachdeva, and I am one of the lawyers for the Prosecution and I will be asking you a couple of questions this morning. Can I first ask you whether you remember giving a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 12th of March, 1997?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And can I ask you, do you also remember giving a statement, another statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 17th of May, 2006?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in the last couple of days, were you given an opportunity to read through those statements with colleagues of mine from the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, on Saturday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And were you able to verify the contents of those statements?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I mean what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could ask for 65 ter 03064 to be shown to the witness and brought up on the screen here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mrs. Gotovac, do you see a -- do you see a statement there in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And on the first page, do you see your signature there?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And if I were to ask you questions today, would the answers that you give under oath be the same as the contents of this statement that you have signed?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that this statement be entered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will admit the statement as P522.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And if I can now ask the court officer to bring up 65 ter 03065, please, and also for that to be shown to the witness in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mrs. Gotovac, do you see there a statement from the 12th of March, 1997?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And, again, the same question: Do you see your signature there on the first page?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And, again, if I were to ask you questions today in court, would your answers reflect the contents of the statement that you have signed?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Well, they would, to the best of my recollection, because 12 years has elapsed. So perhaps I wouldn't use the same word here and there, but I would remember everything and I would say it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that this statement, also, be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P523, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mrs. Gotovac, I just want to ask you a couple of questions so I'm not going to too long. But the statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor pertains to an incident on 24th of May in 1995 at your residence, that is 43 Safeta Hadzica Street. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Safeta Zajke Street. Sorry?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I want to ask you: Did you sustain injuries from the explosion on that day?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I was wounded. I have a medical certificate. The house was -- the house was destroyed. It was terrible, terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If I could ask you very briefly. You said that you were wounded. What type of injury did you suffer?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. A piece of shrapnel was in my body. Well, whatever it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you said that you had a medical certificate. I'm going to show you a record from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If I could that Prosecution Exhibit 427 be brought up on screen and also shown to the witness in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Are you able to see the B/C/S -- the record in a language that you understand in front of you, Mrs. Gotovac?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And can I just confirm that is a certificate of your admission in hospital and confirms the injuries that you sustained from that explosion on that day?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you. And my last question is this: At the place of your residence and in the vicinity of your residence, were there any Bosnian military facilities located there?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: No. I don't know. Well, not in our street. I don't know about further away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And on the day of the explosion, did you see any Bosnian government soldiers in the vicinity of your house?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mrs. Gotovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, that concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. I'm Branislava Isailovic, lawyer with the Paris Bar. I represent General Dragomir Milosevic, the accused in these proceedings, and I'm going to ask you a few questions regarding the statements that you have just discussed with the Prosecutor a minute ago. You made a statement on May -- on May 17th, 2006, which has been given a number, P522. It was the 65 ter document 3064. Do you have this document in front of you? Do you have this statement in front of you? Could you please move to page 2. Just a minute, please. We're waiting for the document to be pulled up on screen?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document is not in e-court, and I'm not sure how long it is going to take to get it there, so we may want to proceed without it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not in e-court. Do you have a hard copy which could be placed on the ELMO? Is that possible with this system?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh, it's not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But I understand that -- sorry, Mr. President. I understand the witness has all the materials down there in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So that the witness should herself have a copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's coming on the screen. No, this is not the right document. Fortunately, we are in no hurry today, so we can accommodate technical problems. We're talking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. I have to correct you on that. We won't proceed efficiently.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we have the right document on screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, I believe that you have had time to read this document. On paragraph 3, page 2 of this document, you are talking about Zuc hill. Could you please look at this paragraph 3. Is it true that your house and that Safeta Zajke Street were located on the hills of Zuc? They were located on Zuc hill?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreter cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please answer.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Well, it's pretty far away from my house, Zuc. It's a hill. I don't know how many kilometres away. It's not very close.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you say that Zuc hill is above you. I mean, probably above your house is probably what you mean.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, a high hill and then behind this hill -- well, there is this hill that is behind my house and then behind that hill is Zuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: What is the name of the hill that is right next to your house?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: I don't know. The street is -- I don't know. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You're also saying that it "was occupied by our troops." On your statement in paragraph 3, you say "was occupied by our troops."

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Well, our neighbourhood was not that exposed at first; later on, it was. Later on, there was lots of shelling, but no snipers though. Where could the snipers be coming from anyway, because this is pretty far away.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Could you confirm today as you said in your statement that the soldiers of the ABiH army were on Zuc hill?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And to go to Zuc hill -- to go up Zuc hill, did they use -- did they go through your road, your street?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the main street. They have to go that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So when you answered the Prosecutor's question by a negative when he asked you if there were any military facilitates, what exactly were you thinking of when you answered that question with a negative?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't in our neighbourhood, you know, because we're down this way. Do you understand what I'm saying? Well, rather, we are sort of downhill, if you look at it that way; on a flat area, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, just a small clarification. I actually asked the witness about facilitates, military facilitates, as opposed to military vehicles; in other words, suggesting some type of permanency in the vicinity. Just to make that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Counsel's question was related to military facilities, as far as I see. Thank you anyhow. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: That is my question: What exactly does "military facilities" mean to you?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: It was farther away from us. I mean, really. I don't know myself. It was father at way from us. At any rate, it wasn't there where we were. There was no military, no nothing. That is the main road, the main street. Well, people pass by, of course, but the positions were further away from us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'll try once more. When you're saying -- when you say "military facility," what springs to mind? Can you tell us exactly what it means for you?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: No facilities. There are no military facilities where we are. I don't know about further away. Positions are where the army is, and the army was up there at Zuc and all around Sarajevo, all of those things are positions for me. All of Sarajevo was surrounded, under siege. All the hills were under siege.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, now, I'll try in B/C/S, one last time. I'll ask in French, I apologise, but I will check the interpretation into B/C/S. "Military facility," and this witness must answer very accurately. So could you please tell the witness about "military facility," not "military" or "facility" but "military facility." Could we get from the witness the exact meaning for her of "military facility."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic. Ms. Isailovic, something needs to be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Facilities, I told you already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- something needs to be made clear. It was you, I believe, who to put to the witness a question that incorporated the term "military facility," but you have been subsequently asking her what she means by "military facility," as though she had initially used the term, and that's not so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me explain. I tried to use my knowledge of B/C/S, so I switched on to the B/C/S channel because it looked like the witness kept answering another question than the one I was asking. And when I listened to the B/C/S, I said "military facility" and what I got in B/C/S were "lines or military objects," which is why the witness always referred to the confrontation line. But now, on, my last try, asking the witness not to do either/or, but to actually put to the witness the word "military facility," I got what I was thinking about on the B/C/S channel. I believe that now the witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let us hear. What is your answer, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're asking me about facilities or what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In the interest of clarity, just put the question again to her.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, I would like you to tell us the meaning of a "military facility," in your mind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, what is the point of asking her that? What is the point of asking her to explain what a military facility is? You would be better off asking her about specific objects; and then it is for the Chamber to determine whether they are military facilities. That's a technical term, and she never used that phrase initially. It is you who put to her a question that incorporated that phrase.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise, but the question came from the Prosecution in the first place, and this is why I wanted to get an answer to my question. I wanted to know what sprang to her mind with these two words, because Mr. Sachdeva asked whether there were military facilities. I believe that what was translated into B/C/S was "military objectives," and she immediately said no, without thinking. And if, when you answer so quickly, you probably understood and have a very clear idea of the question that was asked, which is why I wanted to make this point clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand now. The Prosecutor had used that phrase, and she had answered a question in relation to that phrase, in relation to the question put by the Prosecutor, so you're seeking to have her explain what she meant in the answer that she gave to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. So, Witness, do you understand what has happened? The Prosecutor had put a question to you about military facilities and you answered the question, so counsel is asking what did you mean in the answer you gave the Prosecutor by reference to a military facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
